Researchers investigating the life history of the King weakfish (Macrodon atricauda) have documented that newly hatched larvae emerge from fertilised eggs measuring approximately 0.8 millimeters in diameter, a value derived from direct measurements of pelagic eggs collected during spawning surveys. The wet weight at birth for this species has been calculated based on egg dimensions, yielding an estimate of 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], a remarkably small initial mass characteristic of teleost fishes that produce numerous small pelagic eggs, and one that is broadly comparable to values reported for other small-egg sciaenids such as Cynoscion guatucupa. This low neonatal body mass is consistent with the high fecundity observed in other sciaenid species inhabiting coastal waters of the southwestern Atlantic, where planktonic larval survival depends more on numerical output than on per-offspring investment. Following the process of yolk-sac larva emergence, the developing individuals rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days post-hatching before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The morphological transformation that occurs during early development includes the onset of fin ray ossification and the gradual acquisition of the adult body plan, all of which proceed rapidly in warm coastal nursery grounds where water temperatures typically remain elevated throughout the spawning season.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], female King weakfish have been observed to reach sexual maturity after a relatively extended juvenile period. Females take approximately three years since birth [tp = approximately three years since birth] to reach puberty, a duration that reflects the considerable somatic growth required before gonadal recrudescence can be initiated at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Male conspecifics mature more rapidly, with documented values indicating roughly two years since birth [tp = roughly two years since birth] at puberty under identical thermal conditions at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This sexual dimorphism in maturation timing is a common feature among iteroparous sciaenids and is likely linked to differential energetic allocation strategies between the sexes. Following the onset of gametogenesis, both sexes become reproductively active and participate in annual spawning aggregations, which typically occur in coastal waters during the austral spring and summer months. The protracted juvenile phase observed in females may contribute to the attainment of a larger body size prior to first reproduction, thereby enhancing fecundity in subsequent spawning seasons.

Adult King weakfish are known to achieve a maximum recorded total length of 46 centimeters [Li = 46 centimeters], a measurement that represents the ultimate total length attained by individuals in this commercially important sciaenid population. Field surveys conducted along the southeastern Brazilian coast have confirmed that specimens exceeding this size are exceptionally rare, suggesting that this value approximates the asymptotic length for the species under natural conditions. This moderate body size places Macrodon atricauda among the smaller members of its genus, with congeneric species such as Macrodon ancylodon sometimes reaching slightly larger dimensions in adjacent waters. The growth trajectory leading to this ultimate length is characterized by rapid early development followed by a pronounced deceleration as individuals approach their asymptotic size, a pattern typical of demersal fish species inhabiting warm-temperate marine environments. The species' relatively compact body size may confer advantages in terms of reduced energetic demands for basal maintenance requirements, allowing a greater proportion of assimilated energy to be directed toward reproductive effort and seasonal migrations.

The maximum documented lifespan of King weakfish has been estimated from otolith-based age readings, with the oldest individuals recorded at eight years [am = eight years] when maintained under natural thermal regimes approximating 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This longevity is comparable to that reported for other medium-sized sciaenid fishes inhabiting the same coastal ecosystem, though it is notably shorter than the lifespans observed in certain deepwater congeners that experience reduced metabolic rates at lower ambient temperatures. Age-related mortality in this species appears to increase markedly after the sixth year, with very few individuals surviving beyond the eighth annual spawning cycle. The completion of the lifespan is typically associated with progressive physiological deterioration and reproductive senescence, particularly among iteroparous females that have invested heavily in gamete production over consecutive breeding seasons. Natural mortality rates are influenced by predation pressure from larger piscivorous teleosts and elasmobranchs, as well as by fishing mortality, which selectively removes larger, older individuals from the population and may truncate the age structure in heavily exploited regions.

A comprehensive analysis of reproductive output in Macrodon atricauda has revealed that individual females spawn approximately 600,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 600,000 eggs per year] when water temperatures are maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This annual fecundity is achieved through a combination of roughly 5 to 6 spawning events per year [F_R_i = roughly 5 to 6 spawning events per year], each yielding approximately 100,000 to 120,000 eggs per event [N_R_i = approximately 100,000 to 120,000 eggs per event]. This estimate underscores the species' high fecundity and its reliance on a reproductive strategy that compensates for high rates of egg and larval mortality in the planktonic environment. The observed reproductive rate is consistent with the species' life history position along the fast-slow continuum, as King weakfish exhibit relatively rapid maturation and high fecundity compared to larger, longer-lived sciaenids. The energetic cost of sustaining such elevated egg production is substantial, requiring females to maintain high ingestion rates during the spawning season and to mobilize lipid reserves accumulated during the preceding months. Environmental factors such as water temperature and prey availability modulate the realized reproductive output from year to year, introducing significant interannual variability in recruitment success for this economically important fishery species.
